## PDF page 146

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=146)

```text
                                 CHAPTER ELEVEN



                         EV: MODERATE


The simplified EV formula is great, but it does not account for all possible EV
calculations. If you flip a coin with static payouts, the simplified EV formula
works. If you want to see the outright EV of a single bluff, the simplified EV
formula works. But what if you wanted to calculate the EV of going all-in
preflop? In such a scenario there are actually three possibilities:

   ●   You go all-in and your opponent folds

   ●   You go all-in, get called, and you win the pot

   ●   You go all-in, get called, and you lose the pot

For scenarios like this we need to expand the EV formula to account for every
possibility:

                      E V = F($ P O T ) + C (%W * $ W ) – C (% L * $ L)


You might notice that the same key elements are still here from the simplified
EV formula. But there are new additions including F, C, and $Pot. They are:

   ●   F = how often your opponent folds to your preflop all-in

   ●   C = how often your opponent calls your preflop all-in

   ●   $Pot = the size of the pot before you go all-in

                                        PA G E 1 4 6
```

## PDF page 147

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=147)

```text
                                E V: M O DE R AT E


The good news is that F and C are related in the same way that %W and %L
are related: F + C = 100%. So if you go all-in preflop and suspect that your
opponent will fold 40% of the time, you can figure out C by taking 100%-40%.

Luckily, this formula can be used for more than just calculating the EV of
preflop all-ins. You can use this to calculate any play that offers dead money
that you win when your opponent folds to your aggression, and varying out-
comes when your opponent continues.

These exercises are going to help you practice working through EV calcu-
lations that utilize this format. Half of them are focused on preflop decision
making, and the other half look at river betting so you get a variety of spots.
Just know that these kinds of calculations can happen on any street.

TOOLS TO USE: Most players should do these exercises with pen & paper. If
you would like to use a tool, download and use my “Complex EV” spreadsheet
available at www.splitsuit.pro/sheets

PROCESS: Read the question and discern the key information. Then, fill in
each variable in the formula below it and calculate the EV.




TAKEAWAYS: Notice the impact of the $Pot size in the river betting examples.
As your opponent folds more and allows you to pick up the dead money
uncontested more often, your overall EV can quickly skyrocket. Also pay
attention to the EV compared to the money you are investing to the pot.

GLGL.


                                   PA G E 1 4 7
```

```text
                              CHAPTER TWELVE



                        EV: ADVANCED


Now we will turn up the difficulty.

These exercises explore real situations that you encounter at the table, from
all-ins to estimating the EV of betting multiple streets. Utilize the correct EV
formula and calculate the EV of the proposed play.

TOOLS TO USE: Most players should do these exercises with pen & paper. If
you would like to use a tool, download and use the appropriate spreadsheet
available at www.splitsuit.pro/sheets

PROCESS: Read the question and discern the key information. Then, fill in
each variable in the formula below it and calculate the EV.

TAKEAWAYS: Keep in mind that +EV plays are great, but your paramount
goal is to find the optimal play. The optimal play is the highest EV option. So
when exploring these spots and your own hands, remember that it is very
common to have multiple +EV plays available. Keep exploring when you find
a +EV play and test alternative lines and sizes too. There may be another +EV
play that is even more profitable.

GLGL.




                                      PA G E 1 5 2
```
